source_document: ICAO Doc 9870, Manual on the Prevention of Runway Incursions
text: Any occurrence at an aerodrome involving the incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person on the protected area of a surface designated for the landing and takeoff of aircraft.

source_document: FAA Runway Safety programme
text: Runway incursions are classified by cause as pilot deviations, operational incidents (controller actions) or vehicle and pedestrian deviations, and by severity from A to D.

source_document: FAA Runway Safety programme
text: A landing, attempted landing, line-up or takeoff on a surface other than the one assigned: a wrong runway, a taxiway, a closed runway or the wrong airport.

term: Anomaly: Ground Incursion – Runway or Taxiway
source_document: NASA ASRS coding taxonomy
text: An aircraft, vehicle or person entering a runway or taxiway without authorization, or an aircraft using a taxiway or the wrong runway for landing or takeoff.

source_document: SKYbrary – Runway Excursion
text: An aircraft leaves the runway surface during takeoff or landing, either by veering off the side or by overrunning the end.

source_document: ICAO Global Reporting Format (GRF) for runway surface conditions
text: A runway condition code from 6 (dry) down to 0 reports braking performance on wet or contaminated runways (water, slush, snow, ice), so crews can recompute landing distance.

source_document: NASA ASRS coding taxonomy
text: An aircraft departs the runway surface during the takeoff or landing roll, including overruns after a long or fast landing.

source_document: IATA – Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I)
text: A significant, unintended departure of the aircraft from controlled flight, such as a stall, spin or upset, often following a system malfunction or crew response to erroneous indications.

source_document: SKYbrary – Unreliable Airspeed
text: Erroneous or disagreeing airspeed indications, for example from pitot icing, ice crystals or a blocked pitot tube, which can lead to an upset if the crew follows the wrong indication.

source_document: ICAO Annex 10 – Airborne Collision Avoidance System (ACAS)
text: An ACAS or TCAS indication to the flight crew recommending a vertical manoeuvre to increase separation from conflicting traffic.

source_document: EUROCONTROL – Level bust
text: An unauthorised vertical deviation of more than 300 feet from the cleared flight level or altitude, a common cause of loss of separation and TCAS resolution advisories.

source_document: NASA ASRS coding taxonomy
text: Two aircraft in flight come into conflict or lose separation, including near midair collisions and TCAS events.

source_document: SKYbrary – Clear Air Turbulence
text: Turbulence in cloud-free air, often near jet streams or over mountains, with no visual cue and often not shown on weather radar.

source_document: FAA Advisory Circular 120-88A – Preventing Injuries Caused by Turbulence
text: Passengers and flight attendants are injured in turbulence mainly when standing or not wearing seat belts, and by unsecured carts and galley equipment.

source_document: FAA National Wildlife Strike Database
text: A collision between an aircraft and a bird or other wildlife, including ingestion into an engine, reported with damage and phase of flight.

source_document: 14 CFR 33.76 – Bird ingestion (engine certification)
text: Engines must be shown to withstand the ingestion of birds of defined sizes; large or multiple bird ingestion can damage fan blades and cause surge, loss of thrust, shutdown or fire.

source_document: FAA holdover time guidelines (ground de-icing and anti-icing)
text: The estimated time a de-icing or anti-icing fluid protects aircraft surfaces from frost or ice; if it is exceeded before takeoff, the aircraft must be checked or de-iced again.

source_document: SKYbrary – Hard Landing and Tail Strike
text: A touchdown with a vertical load above limits, a bounced landing, or contact of the tail with the runway during takeoff rotation or landing flare.

source_document: FAA Runway Safety programme
text: A runway incursion caused by a ground vehicle or a person, such as a driver or pedestrian entering a runway without ATC authorization.

source_document: SKYbrary – Crosswind Landings
text: Landing with a wind component across the runway; strong or gusty crosswinds near the aircraft limit increase the risk of lateral runway excursion (veer-off).

source_document: FAA Advisory Circular 120-109A – Stall Prevention and Recovery Training
text: Training to recognise and recover from approaches to stall and full stalls, including during go-arounds with high thrust and pitch.

source_document: FAA Advisory Circular 90-23G – Aircraft Wake Turbulence
text: Vortices from a preceding aircraft, strongest behind heavy aircraft at slow speed, can cause sudden rolls on approach or departure; spacing reduces the risk.

source_document: ICAO Doc 4444 – PANS-ATM (separation minima)
text: Two aircraft come closer than the prescribed separation minima, often after an ATC clearance or instruction puts them in conflict.

source_document: SKYbrary – Hydraulic System Failure
text: Loss of hydraulic fluid or pressure that degrades flight controls, brakes, steering or landing gear, handled with non-normal checklists.

source_document: SKYbrary – Landing Gear Malfunction
text: Failure of a landing gear leg to extend, retract or lock, requiring alternate extension or a landing with gear not fully down.

source_document: 14 CFR 121.354 – Terrain awareness and warning system
text: Airliners must carry a system that warns the crew of terrain, obstacles and excessive descent so they can climb away before impact.

source_document: EASA Safety Information Bulletin 2022-02 – GNSS outages and alterations
text: Interference with satellite navigation signals, by jamming or spoofing, causes loss of GPS position, false positions or false terrain warnings, especially near conflict zones.

source_document: SKYbrary – In-Flight Shutdown
text: An engine is shut down in flight because of a failure or a precautionary indication such as low oil pressure, high vibration or fire.

source_document: FAA Advisory Circular 120-60B – Ground Deicing and Anti-icing Program
text: No takeoff may be made with frost, ice or snow adhering to wings or control surfaces; contamination must be removed before departure.

source_document: ICAO Doc 10117 – Manual on the Legal Aspects of Unruly and Disruptive Passengers
text: A passenger who fails to respect rules of conduct or to follow crew instructions, disturbing good order and discipline on board.

source_document: FAA SAFO – Fire risks from lithium batteries in the cabin
text: Portable electronic devices and power banks can overheat in thermal runaway, producing smoke and fire in the cabin; crew cool the device with water or non-alcoholic liquid.

source_document: SKYbrary – Smoke and Fumes
text: Smoke, fumes or burning smells in the flight deck or cabin, often electrical in origin, handled with oxygen masks and the smoke checklist.

source_document: ICAO Annex 6 – Fuel planning and in-flight fuel management
text: The crew declares MINIMUM FUEL when any change may land them below final reserve, and MAYDAY FUEL when the landing fuel is expected to be below final reserve.

source_document: IATA Ground Operations Manual – Pushback and towing
text: Moving an aircraft with a tug or towbar, with wing walkers and headset communication, to prevent collisions with aircraft, vehicles and objects.

source_document: SKYbrary – Tailstrike
text: The aft fuselage contacts the runway during takeoff rotation or landing, often after early rotation, wrong takeoff speeds or excessive pitch.

source_document: FAA Advisory Circular 00-54 – Pilot Windshear Guide
text: Sudden changes in wind speed or direction near the ground, such as microbursts from thunderstorms, causing airspeed loss; crews fly the windshear escape manoeuvre.

source_document: SKYbrary – Landing Short (Undershoot)
text: The aircraft touches down before the runway threshold, often after an unstable or low approach or a visual illusion.

source_document: FAA Advisory Circular 91-74B – Pilot Guide: Flight in Icing Conditions
text: Ice accumulates on wings, tail and windshield in supercooled cloud or freezing drizzle, increasing drag and stall speed.

source_document: FAA National Wildlife Strike Database – strike reporting
text: A collision with birds that damages the aircraft, such as a cracked windshield, dented radome or ingested engine, reported to the wildlife strike database.

source_document: FAA Runway Safety programme – Pilot deviation
text: A runway incursion caused by a pilot, such as crossing a hold-short line or entering a runway without an ATC clearance.

source_document: SKYbrary – Lateral Navigation Error
text: The aircraft leaves its cleared route because of a wrong route, waypoint or procedure loaded in the flight management system.

source_document: ECCAIRS 1.3.0.12 · Events (390) · 2220600 · Aircraft operation general › Weather encounters
text: Encounter with any or all of a) clear air turbulence (CAT) b) turbulence in cloud c) vortex / wake turbulence also to be used in events in which the aircraft was damaged by turbulence. CAT: Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) is the bumpiness experienced by aircraft at high altitudes (above 18,000 feet) in either cloud- free conditions or in stratiform clouds. CAT occurs when undulations (known as gravity waves) in the upper atmosphere become steep and unstable, then break down into chaotic motion. The scale of wave motion that normally affects jet aircraft is on the order of ~10 meters to ~1-2 kilometers. These unstable waves occur when vertical wind shear becomes locally excessive, allowing the waves to overcome the stability of environmental temperature conditions. This condition is known as Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. Most CAT occurs on the fringes of (not within the core of) the jet stream, in the vicinity of upper level frontal zones where temperature contrasts are strong. CAT may also occur when strong winds cross a mountain range in certain thermal conditions, allowing gravity waves to amplify and propagate vertically toward the stratosphere. These 'mountain waves' may be smooth undulations, resulting in updrafts and downdrafts (UDDF in pilot report code), or can break down into smaller scale turbulence. A third instance in which CAT occurs is when strong winds encounter the tops of thunderstorm clouds, resulting in strong shear waves that extend well downstream from the convective cloud.

source_document: ECCAIRS 1.3.0.12 · Events (390) · 2220400 · Aircraft operation general › Weather encounters
text: Wake turbulence: Turbulent air behind an aircraft caused by any of the following: (a) wing-tip vortices; (b) rotor-tip vortices; (c) jet-engine thrust stream or jet blast; (d) rotor downwash; (e) prop wash. Wing tip vortex: A circular pattern of air current created by the movement of an airfoil through the air when the airfoil is generating lift. As an airfoil moves through the atmosphere in sustained flight, an area of high pressure is created beneath it and an area of low pressure is created above it. The air flowing from the high-pressure area to the low-pressure area around and about the tips of the airfoil tends to roll up into two rapidly rotating vortices, cylindrical in shape. These vortices are the predominant parts of aircraft wake turbulence and their rotational force is dependent upon the wing loading, gross weight, and speed of the generating aircraft. The vortices from medium to heavy aircraft can be of extremely high velocity and hazardous to smaller aircraft.

text: (ATA Code:7830) An event involving the airframe furnished system and components mounted at turbo-jet engine exhaust tailpipes to direct engine thrust forward for deceleration.
